**Bon** "**John**" **Phan** (born October 10, 1974, in Da Nang, Vietnam) is a Vietnamese-American professional poker player based in Stockton, California,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Phan#cite_note-1) who is a two-time World Series of Poker bracelet winner[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Phan#cite_note-results-2) and is a winner and four-time final tablist of World Poker Tour Championships.

## World Series of Poker
[edit]
Phan has made numerous World Series of Poker (WSOP) money finishes, including the final table of the $5,000 Seven-card stud event in 2005, finished fourth and outlasted both professional poker players Dave Colclough and Rob Hollink.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Phan#cite_note-3)
At the 2006 WSOP, Phan finished second in the $1,000 No-Limit Hold'em event when his **Q♠5♠** failed to improve against Jon Friedberg's **A♥7♥** on a board of **10♥9♦3♠2♥7♠**.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Phan#cite_note-4) Phan earned $289,389 for his runner-up finish. The next year at the 2007 World Series of Poker Phan was runner-up to Francois Safieddine in the $2,500 No Limit Hold'em event, earning $330,846 but it was not until the 2008 World Series of Poker that Phan won his first bracelet after winning the $3,000 No-Limit Hold'em event, earning $434,789 and then he won his second bracelet the same year, this time in the $2,500 2-7 Triple Draw event, earning $151,896. Phan cashed for a total of $608,464 at the 2008 WSOP.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Phan#cite_note-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Phan#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Phan#cite_note-7)

## World Series of Poker
### World Series of Poker bracelets
[edit]
| Year | Event | Prize Money |  
| --- | --- | --- |  
| 2008 | $3,000 No-Limit[Hold'em](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_hold_'em "Texas hold 'em") | $434,789 |  
| 2008 | $2,500 2-7 Triple Draw | $151,896 |
Phan cashed eleven times on the World Poker Tour (WPT) making the final table in four of them, one was at the $25,000 WPT Championship of season 3, receiving $518,920 for finishing in fourth place above Hollink, Phil Ivey, Joe Beevers, Chris Ferguson and Juha Helppi.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Phan#cite_note-8) The other was at the $9,600 No Limit Hold'em WPT season 6 event at the 2008 Bay 101 Shooting Stars where he finished 6th, earning $135,000.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Phan#cite_note-9) In July 2008, Phan made another WPT final table finishing in fifth place at the Bellagio Cup IV, earning $193,915[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Phan#cite_note-Cardplayer-10)
On the WPT seventh season, Phan won his first WPT title after defeating well known online player Amit "Amak316″ Makhija during heads-up play, winning the WPT bracelet and over $1.1 million at the Legends of Poker held at The Bicycle Casino in Bell Gardens, California.
John Phan at Nicky Hilton's poker tournament[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Phan#cite_note-11)

## World Series of Poker
### World Series of Poker bracelets
Phan won two events at The Fifth Annual Jack Binion World Poker Open in 2004, the $500 Limit Hold'em event, earning $160,965 and $500 Pot Limit Hold'em event, earning $85,257 also cashing three other times at that same event.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Phan#cite_note-12)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Phan#cite_note-13) He later won the $3,000 No Limit Hold'em event at the Festa al Lago II in 2004, earning $189,900.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Phan#cite_note-14) He won the $2,425 No Limit Hold'em event at the 2005 L.A. Poker Classic, earning $300,578 and was runner-up to Marcel Lüske in the $3,000 No Limit Hold'em event at the Fourth Annual Five-Star World Poker Classic in 2006, earning $179,195.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Phan#cite_note-15)
As of 2017, his total live tournament winnings exceed $5,525,000.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Phan#cite_note-results-2) His 29 cashes as the WSOP account for over $1,450,000 of those winnings.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Phan#cite_note-16)
He was the Cardplayer Magazine 2008 Player of the Year with 6,704 points as well as 2008 Bluff Magazine Player of the Year.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Phan#cite_note-17)

He focuses on the linguistic history of Vietnam and its cultural context. . His first book, The Lost Tongues of the Red River: Annamese Middle Chinese & the Origins of the Vietnamese Language, published in April 2025 by Harvard University Press, posits the existence of a regional dialect of Middle Chinese once spoken in northern Vietnam (the Red River Delta) and explores how this dialect influenced the emergence of Vietnamese Phan completed his M.A. at Columbia University (on Ming‑Qing vernacular fiction, 2005) and earned his Ph.D. from Cornell (on Sino‑Vietnamese language contact, 2012). **Bon** "**John**" **Phan** (born October 10, 1974, in Da Nang, Vietnam) is a Vietnamese-American professional poker player based in Stockton, California,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Phan#cite_note-1) who is a two-time World Series of Poker bracelet winner[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Phan#cite_note-results-2) and is a winner and four-time final tablist of World Poker Tour Championships.
texts.1:
## World Series of Poker
[edit]
Phan has made numerous World Series of Poker (WSOP) money finishes, including the final table of the $5,000 Seven-card stud event in 2005, finished fourth and outlasted both professional poker players Dave Colclough and Rob Hollink.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Phan#cite_note-3)
At the 2006 WSOP, Phan finished second in the $1,000 No-Limit Hold'em event when his **Q♠5♠** failed to improve against Jon Friedberg's **A♥7♥** on a board of **10♥9♦3♠2♥7♠**.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Phan#cite_note-4) Phan earned $289,389 for his runner-up finish. The next year at the 2007 World Series of Poker Phan was runner-up to Francois Safieddine in the $2,500 No Limit Hold'em event, earning $330,846 but it was not until the 2008 World Series of Poker that Phan won his first bracelet after winning the $3,000 No-Limit Hold'em event, earning $434,789 and then he won his second bracelet the same year, this time in the $2,500 2-7 Triple Draw event, earning $151,896. Phan cashed for a total of $608,464 at the 2008 WSOP.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Phan#cite_note-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Phan#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Phan#cite_note-7)

John D. Phan is an Associate Professor of Vietnamese Humanities at Columbia University, based in the Department of East Asian Languages & Cultures and the Weatherhead East Asian Institute. He focuses on the linguistic history of Vietnam and its cultural context. . His first book, The Lost Tongues of the Red River: Annamese Middle Chinese & the Origins of the Vietnamese Language, published in April 2025 by Harvard University Press, posits the existence of a regional dialect of Middle Chinese once spoken in northern Vietnam (the Red River Delta) and explores how this dialect influenced the emergence of Vietnamese Phan completed his M.A. at Columbia University (on Ming‑Qing vernacular fiction, 2005) and earned his Ph.D. from Cornell (on Sino‑Vietnamese language contact, 2012). His scholarship examines the evolution of writing systems, vernacular literary forms (like chữ Nôm), and the social-political implications of multilingualism in East Asia In this episode, Kenneth sits down with John to talk about his new book The Lost Tongues of the Red River. They get into the role language plays in shaping who we are—not just how we speak, but how we think, remember, and connect to culture. John shares insights into the roots of the Vietnamese language, how it’s evolved, and what might be slipping away. They also dig into the experience of growing up speaking English instead of Vietnamese, and what that means for identity, especially in the diaspora. It’s a thoughtful, wide-ranging conversation about language, memory, and what it really means to be Vietnamese—wherever you are in the world.…...more

**Bon** "**John**" **Phan** (born October 10, 1974, in Da Nang, Vietnam) is a Vietnamese-American professional poker player based in Stockton, California,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Phan#cite_note-1) who is a two-time World Series of Poker bracelet winner[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Phan#cite_note-results-2) and is a winner and four-time final tablist of World Poker Tour Championships.

Phan has made numerous World Series of Poker (WSOP) money finishes, including the final table of the $5,000 Seven-card stud event in 2005, finished fourth and outlasted both professional poker players Dave Colclough and Rob Hollink.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Phan#cite_note-3)
At the 2006 WSOP, Phan finished second in the $1,000 No-Limit Hold'em event when his **Q♠5♠** failed to improve against Jon Friedberg's **A♥7♥** on a board of **10♥9♦3♠2♥7♠**.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Phan#cite_note-4) Phan earned $289,389 for his runner-up finish. The next year at the 2007 World Series of Poker Phan was runner-up to Francois Safieddine in the $2,500 No Limit Hold'em event, earning $330,846 but it was not until the 2008 World Series of Poker that Phan won his first bracelet after winning the $3,000 No-Limit Hold'em event, earning $434,789 and then he won his second bracelet the same year, this time in the $2,500 2-7 Triple Draw event, earning $151,896. Phan cashed for a total of $608,464 at the 2008 WSOP.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Phan#cite_note-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Phan#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Phan#cite_note-7)

## One glance at the Pu Luong Nature Reserve and you’ll see why the ethnic Thai people made this enchanting valley their home long ago. The slow pace in Pu Luong is a striking contrast to life in the capital just a few hours away. Endless mountains, fertile valleys and pristine jungle are just a few good reasons to visit. Here are seven ways to make the most of your time in this beautiful destination.
Chapter 01 —

## Take a swim in Thác Hiêu Waterfall
From the top of Hieu village, it’s only a short hike through the rice fields before you’re presented with a series of dreamy waterfalls cascading down the hillside. Climb down and follow along to where the two streams meet and the pools become larger. This is the perfect spot to cool down with a quick dip, relax in nature, and explore different sections of the falls.
Chapter 02 —

## Pay a visit to an ethnic Thai Village
****
Pu Luong is dotted with quaint hamlets and villages throughout the park, each with its own unique history. Most of the communities in the reserve are Thai people, an ethnic group with two local branches, White Thai and Black Thai. The Thai people are highly skilled at wet rice cultivation and their homes are built in a raised stilt style. Staying at one of these homestays is a fantastic way to experience local customs and see what life is like for this Vietnamese minority.
Chapter 03 —

## Immerse yourself in nature
Pu Luong’s mountains are covered with tropical rainforest, while the valley is a series of cultivated rice terraces. Take a walk along the valley floor or in the foothills to get up close with the area’s flora and fauna. Listen to the waterwheels and forest sounds, wave at farmers and grazing water buffalo, and snap pictures of the greenery and wildlife. Simply being in Pu Luong Nature Reserve is a breath of fresh air.
Chapter 04 —

## Join a craft workshop
Long-established ways of living have been passed down for generations in Pu Luong. The Thai people have kept the habits of their ancestors as an important part of their culture and community. Weaving, embroidery, basket making and bamboo furniture are all key skills for the Thai people. Take the opportunity to learn about any these traditions with a craft workshop during your stay. You’ll not only learn something new but also support local enterprise and help preserve these timeless traditions.

## 1. Overview of Pu Luong Nature Reserve
Pu Luong Nature Reserve spans 17,662 hectares across both Quan Hoa and Ba Thuoc districts in Thanh Hoa province, with two-thirds of the reserve consisting primarily of tropical forest. Translated as the "highest peak of the village" in Thai, Pu Luong is renowned as the home to the Thai and Muong ethnic groups who have cultivated this landscape for centuries. This remarkable destination features dense forests, cascading waterfalls, mysterious caves, and the iconic terraced rice fields that cascade down mountainsides like green staircases.
The reserve stands out as having the biggest forest area on Karst terrain in Northern Vietnam, containing three distinct types of forest ecosystems. Beyond its natural beauty, Pu Luong Eco Garden Vietnam offers visitors an authentic glimpse into traditional Vietnamese highland culture, where ancient farming techniques and time-honored customs continue to thrive in harmony with the pristine environment.
_Pu Luong’s mountains are blanketed in tropical rainforest, while its valleys unfold into cascading terraces of cultivated rice fields (Source: Canva)_

## 2. How to get to Pu Luong Vietnam
The travel distance from Hanoi to Pu Luong is approximately 180km, with three main roads providing access to the Reserve. Whether you prefer the independence of self-driving or the convenience of public transport, multiple options ensure you can reach this natural paradise.

## 2. How to get to Pu Luong Vietnam
### 2.1. By Motorbike or Private Car
Riding a motorbike is the best way to get around Pu Luong, allowing you to explore the area and reach more remote villages, though travelers should exercise caution as some roads can be rough and narrow.
Motorbike rentals typically cost VND 100,000 - VND 150,000 (USD 3.8 - USD 5.8) per day, while private car rentals range from VND 1,500,000 - VND 1,700,000 (USD 60 - USD 70) per one-way trip, depending on vehicle type and rental duration. Below are some route options:
*   **Hanoi - Ho Chi Minh Trail - Cam Thuy - Canh Nang (Ba Thuoc) - Pu Luong:** This 180km journey takes approximately 4 - 5 hours, following the historic Ho Chi Minh Trail through scenic mountain passes and traditional villages.  
*   **Hanoi - Hoa Binh - Mai Chau - Pu Luong**: A 160km route taking 3.5 - 4 hours, this path offers stunning valley views and passes through the famous Mai Chau valley with its White Thai settlements.  
*   **Hanoi - Tan Lac - Son Ba Muoi - Pu Luong:** The shortest route at 140km (3 - 3.5 hours), this road cuts through the heart of the mountainous region, offering dramatic landscapes and fewer tourist crowds. Make sure to follow Pu Luong Vietnam map so that you won’t get lost.
_For adventure seekers with solid riding experience, renting a motorbike is a budget-friendly and flexible option to explore Pu Luong at your own pace_ _(Source: Pexels)_

## 2. How to get to Pu Luong Vietnam
### 2.2. By Bus
For travelers unfamiliar with the roads or seeking budget-friendly options, daily limousine buses depart from Hanoi's Old Quarter to Pu Luong. The journey typically takes 4 - 5 hours, with ticket prices around VND 300,000 (USD 11.5) per person. This option provides comfort and safety while allowing you to enjoy the scenery without navigation concerns.

## 3. Best Time to Visit Pu Luong Nature Reserve
The best time to visit Pu Luong is during the two rice field seasons from May to June and from September to October. During these periods, the terraced fields showcase their most spectacular colors, vibrant green in the growing season and golden yellow during harvest time.
The dry season from November to February offers cooler temperatures ideal for hiking, though the rice terraces appear less dramatic. Avoid the rainy season (July - August) when paths become slippery and the weather is unpredictable, unless you're specifically seeking the lush, misty atmosphere of the monsoon months.
_Golden rice terraces during harvest season in Pu Luong Nature Reserve_ _(Source: Canva)_

## 4. What to Do in Pu Luong Nature Reserve Vietnam
The reserve offers an incredible array of activities that showcase both its natural wonders and rich cultural heritage. From challenging mountain treks to peaceful village encounters, every experience provides unique insights into this remarkable ecosystem.

## 4. What to Do in Pu Luong Nature Reserve Vietnam
### 4.1. Trek to The Summit of The Mountain for A Spectacular View
The mountain terrain, covered with humid tropical forests, contrasts beautifully with the valley's cultivated terraced rice fields below. Embark on hiking trails that wind through the valley floor and foothills, bringing you closer to the region's diverse flora and fauna. As you ascend, listen to the gentle sounds of traditional hydraulic wheels and forest wildlife while observing residents engaged in their daily rice field activities.
The journey rewards photographers with stunning opportunities to capture the area's greenery and wildlife, culminating in breathtaking panoramic views from the summit that showcase the full majesty of this pristine landscape.
_Panoramic mountain views from Pu Luong's highest peaks_ _(Source: Canva)_

## 4. What to Do in Pu Luong Nature Reserve Vietnam
### 4.2. Take A Refreshing Swim at Hieu Waterfall
Situated in Hieu village, this magnificent cascading waterfall plunges approximately 800 meters, creating natural swimming pools perfect for relaxation and enjoying a peaceful snack break. The waterfall's multiple tiers provide various vantage points for photography and contemplation.
Getting to the waterfall is straightforward with a motorbike, as you can park close to the falls for less than VND 26,000 (USD 1). Car travelers will need to park near the entrance due to narrow access roads and walk approximately 10 minutes through scenic forest paths to reach this refreshing natural wonder.
_Crystal-clear waters at the 800-meter Hieu Waterfall in Pu Luong_ _(Source: Canva)_

## 4. What to Do in Pu Luong Nature Reserve Vietnam
### 4.3. Meet The Ethnic Minorities
The majority of communities within the reserve are Thai people, an ethnic group comprising two local branches: White Thai and Black Thai. These communities demonstrate remarkable skill in wet rice cultivation techniques passed down through generations, and their traditional homes showcase the distinctive raised stilt architecture adapted to the mountainous terrain.
Staying at one of the authentic homestays operated by these families provides an extraordinary opportunity to experience local customs firsthand, participate in daily activities, and gain a deeper understanding of their sustainable relationship with the natural environment.
_Traditional Thai stilt houses rise above the valley floor in Pu Luong, showcasing the distinctive architecture of local ethnic communities_ _(Source: Canva)_

## 4. What to Do in Pu Luong Nature Reserve Vietnam
### 4.4. Shop for Unique Souvenirs from Pho Doan Market
Operating every Thursday and Sunday morning, Pho Doan Market serves as a vibrant gathering place where local ethnic minorities including the Muong and Thai communities converge to buy and trade their goods. This colorful market offers an impressive variety of authentic items, from intricately handmade crafts and traditional clothing to region-specific products like aromatic spices and medicinal herbs.
The market atmosphere buzzes with local languages and provides excellent opportunities to interact with friendly vendors while discovering unique souvenirs that reflect the area's rich cultural heritage.
_Colorful displays of handmade crafts, traditional textiles, and local spices fill the bustling Pho Doan Market_ _(Source: Canva)_

## 4. What to Do in Pu Luong Nature Reserve Vietnam
### 4.5 Explore The Mysterious Bat Cave
Bat Cave (Hang Doi) represents the most remarkable geological formation in Pu Luong, having required more than 250 million years to achieve its current magnificent shape. Natural forces gradually wore down the surrounding karst landscape, leaving this striking feature carved deep within the central core of a river system. The same river that sculpted the cave continues to support local agriculture by providing essential water to the villages of Kho Muong and Ban Pon.
Within this mysterious cavern, several different bat species make their home, occasionally visible flying overhead. These bats play crucial roles in maintaining the area's ecological balance through insect population control and seed dispersal throughout the reserve.

### Pu Luong
Pu Luong District, and the national park of the same name, comprises a rugged, mountainous region situated some 160 kilometres southwest of Hanoi, close to the present-day border with Laos. The Park – officially categorised as a nature reserve, we believe – consists of alternate steep, forest-covered limestone ridges and lush, rice terrace-filled valleys. Villages nestled at the foot of the ridges are home to people of the White and Black Tai ethnic groups. (Distant cousins of modern-day Thais, Tai refers to the ethnic/linguistic group rather than the nationality, with such groups inhabiting a wide swathe of mountains in northwestern Vietnam.)
Black Tai farmers, further north near Dien Bien Phu District
The steep slopes mean that outside of the cultivated valleys, extensive forest cover remains intact and the nature reserve lays claim to no less than 250 bird species as well as numerous mammal and reptile species.
Although traditionally a somewhat remote, off-the-beaten-track destination, access – i.e. the road infrastructure – has improved of late and Pu Luong’s spectacular scenery, homestays and eco-resorts are beginning to attract the more adventurous kind of visitors – both local and foreign.
As the area lies conveniently close to the Lao-Vietnamese border at Na Meo, Pu Luong has featured on our Laos and Vietnam tours (both Mountains and Hilltribes and Unexplored, the Far North) for some time. The tours takes us overland from the World Heritage Plain of Jars in northeastern Laos to Sam Nuea District and on to the border before winding through parts of northern Vietnam, including Pu Luong and the celebrated rice terraces of Mu Cang Chai, to finish in the capital, Hanoi.
Pu Luong – the landscape of forested hills and rice terrace-filled valleys is too good to miss
We’ve also, in the past, organised trips to Pu Luong as extensions from Hanoi and the consistently awesome feedback has encouraged us to slot the destination into our popular Hanoi to Saigon as well as our Vietnam World Heritage tours. Both kicking off in Hanoi, these tours travel from north to south and while Mu Cang Chai is just too far out of the way, Pu Luong does lend itself to inclusion on a loop: Hanoi, Halong, Ninh Binh, Mai Chau, Pu Luong, Hanoi.

### Pu Luong
Halong to Ninh Binh is a comfortable morning’s drive, allowing for a late afternoon leisurely rowing boat tour of the World Heritage landscapes of Trang An with an overnight stay at the charming, family-run Nan’s House in Tam Coc. The following morning we then head west to Pu Luong with a break at the scenic town of Mai Chau for lunch and a cycle along the quiet lanes of the surrounding valley.
Scenically located Mai Chau Town for lunch and a chance to stretch our legs
Our new Pu Luong section thus includes two nights at a beautifully situated eco resort and a full day’s exploration of the surrounding area with a nature and village hike and, water levels permitting, a boat trip down one of the area’s picturesque rivers. The following morning will provide some time at leisure; relax and admire the eco-resort’s poolside views or some optional additional hiking for the more energetic.The afternoon is a return drive to Hanoi to catch the night sleeper train south to Dong Hoi and further adventures in Phong Nha – Ke Bang, Vietnam’s largest, and now World Heritage-listed national park.
Not too shabby! The eco-resort bar and pool at Pu Luong.
As we said, Pu Luong is just too good to miss and our itinerary tweaking adds what is undoubtedly one of Vietnam’s highlights to what, if we do say so ourselves, were already excellent tours.

## One glance at the Pu Luong Nature Reserve and you’ll see why the ethnic Thai people made this enchanting valley their home long ago. The slow pace in Pu Luong is a striking contrast to life in the capital just a few hours away. Endless mountains, fertile valleys and pristine jungle are just a few good reasons to visit. Here are seven ways to make the most of your time in this beautiful destination.
Chapter 01 —

## Take a swim in Thác Hiêu Waterfall
From the top of Hieu village, it’s only a short hike through the rice fields before you’re presented with a series of dreamy waterfalls cascading down the hillside. Climb down and follow along to where the two streams meet and the pools become larger. This is the perfect spot to cool down with a quick dip, relax in nature, and explore different sections of the falls.
Chapter 02 —

## Pay a visit to an ethnic Thai Village
****
Pu Luong is dotted with quaint hamlets and villages throughout the park, each with its own unique history. Most of the communities in the reserve are Thai people, an ethnic group with two local branches, White Thai and Black Thai. The Thai people are highly skilled at wet rice cultivation and their homes are built in a raised stilt style. Staying at one of these homestays is a fantastic way to experience local customs and see what life is like for this Vietnamese minority.
Chapter 03 —

## Immerse yourself in nature
Pu Luong’s mountains are covered with tropical rainforest, while the valley is a series of cultivated rice terraces. Take a walk along the valley floor or in the foothills to get up close with the area’s flora and fauna. Listen to the waterwheels and forest sounds, wave at farmers and grazing water buffalo, and snap pictures of the greenery and wildlife. Simply being in Pu Luong Nature Reserve is a breath of fresh air.
Chapter 04 —

## Join a craft workshop
Long-established ways of living have been passed down for generations in Pu Luong. The Thai people have kept the habits of their ancestors as an important part of their culture and community. Weaving, embroidery, basket making and bamboo furniture are all key skills for the Thai people. Take the opportunity to learn about any these traditions with a craft workshop during your stay. You’ll not only learn something new but also support local enterprise and help preserve these timeless traditions.
Chapter 05 —

## Dine on farm-to-table home cooking
Chapter 06 —
There’s nothing more delightful than food made from ingredients grown right in the area. Pu Luong is home to an amazing array of vegetables such as baby pumpkin leaf, green beans and bamboo shoots. With so many freshly harvested options, you’re likely to find a few new favourites on the table. For a real Pu Luong lunch or dinner, try the locally raised pork and grilled mountain snails dipped in fish sauce.
Chapter 07 —

## Trek to the top of Mt. Pu Luong
Trekking is the best way to soak up the natural splendour of Pu Luong. Access to maps and marked trails are limited throughout the park, so hiring a local guide will save you time and help you plot the perfect route. You may like to hike to the summit of Mt. Pu Luong, or do a multi-day trek through the entire reserve. Either way, you’re in a for an exhilarating experience.
Chapter 08 —

## Enjoy an authentic homestay
Homestays make up the majority of accommodation options in Pu Luong. The good news is, each one is secluded and tranquil and you can take your pick from mountainside huts to stilted homes in the rice terraces. While there are also a handful of retreats, lodges and even treehouses on offer, homestays will give you a memorable experience deep in the serenity of the reserve.
Chapter 09 —

## Transport to Pu Luong
Pu Luong is about 150 kilometres from Ha Noi, and takes approximately four and half hours to reach by car. Travellers can also hire private shuttles from Ha Noi, with a stop in Mai Chau along the way. There is no direct public buses from Ha Noi but there are buses to Mai Chau from My Dinh bus station, where you can take a taxi for the remaining 90-minute drive to Pu Luong.

### Pu Luong
Pu Luong District, and the national park of the same name, comprises a rugged, mountainous region situated some 160 kilometres southwest of Hanoi, close to the present-day border with Laos. The Park – officially categorised as a nature reserve, we believe – consists of alternate steep, forest-covered limestone ridges and lush, rice terrace-filled valleys. Villages nestled at the foot of the ridges are home to people of the White and Black Tai ethnic groups. (Distant cousins of modern-day Thais, Tai refers to the ethnic/linguistic group rather than the nationality, with such groups inhabiting a wide swathe of mountains in northwestern Vietnam.)
Black Tai farmers, further north near Dien Bien Phu District
The steep slopes mean that outside of the cultivated valleys, extensive forest cover remains intact and the nature reserve lays claim to no less than 250 bird species as well as numerous mammal and reptile species.
Although traditionally a somewhat remote, off-the-beaten-track destination, access – i.e. the road infrastructure – has improved of late and Pu Luong’s spectacular scenery, homestays and eco-resorts are beginning to attract the more adventurous kind of visitors – both local and foreign.
As the area lies conveniently close to the Lao-Vietnamese border at Na Meo, Pu Luong has featured on our Laos and Vietnam tours (both Mountains and Hilltribes and Unexplored, the Far North) for some time. The tours takes us overland from the World Heritage Plain of Jars in northeastern Laos to Sam Nuea District and on to the border before winding through parts of northern Vietnam, including Pu Luong and the celebrated rice terraces of Mu Cang Chai, to finish in the capital, Hanoi.
Pu Luong – the landscape of forested hills and rice terrace-filled valleys is too good to miss
We’ve also, in the past, organised trips to Pu Luong as extensions from Hanoi and the consistently awesome feedback has encouraged us to slot the destination into our popular Hanoi to Saigon as well as our Vietnam World Heritage tours. Both kicking off in Hanoi, these tours travel from north to south and while Mu Cang Chai is just too far out of the way, Pu Luong does lend itself to inclusion on a loop: Hanoi, Halong, Ninh Binh, Mai Chau, Pu Luong, Hanoi.

### Pu Luong
Halong to Ninh Binh is a comfortable morning’s drive, allowing for a late afternoon leisurely rowing boat tour of the World Heritage landscapes of Trang An with an overnight stay at the charming, family-run Nan’s House in Tam Coc. The following morning we then head west to Pu Luong with a break at the scenic town of Mai Chau for lunch and a cycle along the quiet lanes of the surrounding valley.
Scenically located Mai Chau Town for lunch and a chance to stretch our legs
Our new Pu Luong section thus includes two nights at a beautifully situated eco resort and a full day’s exploration of the surrounding area with a nature and village hike and, water levels permitting, a boat trip down one of the area’s picturesque rivers. The following morning will provide some time at leisure; relax and admire the eco-resort’s poolside views or some optional additional hiking for the more energetic.The afternoon is a return drive to Hanoi to catch the night sleeper train south to Dong Hoi and further adventures in Phong Nha – Ke Bang, Vietnam’s largest, and now World Heritage-listed national park.
Not too shabby! The eco-resort bar and pool at Pu Luong.
As we said, Pu Luong is just too good to miss and our itinerary tweaking adds what is undoubtedly one of Vietnam’s highlights to what, if we do say so ourselves, were already excellent tours.

## 1. Overview of Pu Luong Nature Reserve
Pu Luong Nature Reserve spans 17,662 hectares across both Quan Hoa and Ba Thuoc districts in Thanh Hoa province, with two-thirds of the reserve consisting primarily of tropical forest. Translated as the "highest peak of the village" in Thai, Pu Luong is renowned as the home to the Thai and Muong ethnic groups who have cultivated this landscape for centuries. This remarkable destination features dense forests, cascading waterfalls, mysterious caves, and the iconic terraced rice fields that cascade down mountainsides like green staircases.
The reserve stands out as having the biggest forest area on Karst terrain in Northern Vietnam, containing three distinct types of forest ecosystems. Beyond its natural beauty, Pu Luong Eco Garden Vietnam offers visitors an authentic glimpse into traditional Vietnamese highland culture, where ancient farming techniques and time-honored customs continue to thrive in harmony with the pristine environment.
_Pu Luong’s mountains are blanketed in tropical rainforest, while its valleys unfold into cascading terraces of cultivated rice fields (Source: Canva)_

## 2. How to get to Pu Luong Vietnam
The travel distance from Hanoi to Pu Luong is approximately 180km, with three main roads providing access to the Reserve. Whether you prefer the independence of self-driving or the convenience of public transport, multiple options ensure you can reach this natural paradise.

## 2. How to get to Pu Luong Vietnam
### 2.1. By Motorbike or Private Car
Riding a motorbike is the best way to get around Pu Luong, allowing you to explore the area and reach more remote villages, though travelers should exercise caution as some roads can be rough and narrow.
Motorbike rentals typically cost VND 100,000 - VND 150,000 (USD 3.8 - USD 5.8) per day, while private car rentals range from VND 1,500,000 - VND 1,700,000 (USD 60 - USD 70) per one-way trip, depending on vehicle type and rental duration. Below are some route options:
*   **Hanoi - Ho Chi Minh Trail - Cam Thuy - Canh Nang (Ba Thuoc) - Pu Luong:** This 180km journey takes approximately 4 - 5 hours, following the historic Ho Chi Minh Trail through scenic mountain passes and traditional villages.  
*   **Hanoi - Hoa Binh - Mai Chau - Pu Luong**: A 160km route taking 3.5 - 4 hours, this path offers stunning valley views and passes through the famous Mai Chau valley with its White Thai settlements.  
*   **Hanoi - Tan Lac - Son Ba Muoi - Pu Luong:** The shortest route at 140km (3 - 3.5 hours), this road cuts through the heart of the mountainous region, offering dramatic landscapes and fewer tourist crowds. Make sure to follow Pu Luong Vietnam map so that you won’t get lost.
_For adventure seekers with solid riding experience, renting a motorbike is a budget-friendly and flexible option to explore Pu Luong at your own pace_ _(Source: Pexels)_

## 2. How to get to Pu Luong Vietnam
### 2.2. By Bus
For travelers unfamiliar with the roads or seeking budget-friendly options, daily limousine buses depart from Hanoi's Old Quarter to Pu Luong. The journey typically takes 4 - 5 hours, with ticket prices around VND 300,000 (USD 11.5) per person. This option provides comfort and safety while allowing you to enjoy the scenery without navigation concerns.

## 3. Best Time to Visit Pu Luong Nature Reserve
The best time to visit Pu Luong is during the two rice field seasons from May to June and from September to October. During these periods, the terraced fields showcase their most spectacular colors, vibrant green in the growing season and golden yellow during harvest time.
The dry season from November to February offers cooler temperatures ideal for hiking, though the rice terraces appear less dramatic. Avoid the rainy season (July - August) when paths become slippery and the weather is unpredictable, unless you're specifically seeking the lush, misty atmosphere of the monsoon months.
_Golden rice terraces during harvest season in Pu Luong Nature Reserve_ _(Source: Canva)_

## 4. What to Do in Pu Luong Nature Reserve Vietnam
The reserve offers an incredible array of activities that showcase both its natural wonders and rich cultural heritage. From challenging mountain treks to peaceful village encounters, every experience provides unique insights into this remarkable ecosystem.

## 4. What to Do in Pu Luong Nature Reserve Vietnam
### 4.1. Trek to The Summit of The Mountain for A Spectacular View
The mountain terrain, covered with humid tropical forests, contrasts beautifully with the valley's cultivated terraced rice fields below. Embark on hiking trails that wind through the valley floor and foothills, bringing you closer to the region's diverse flora and fauna. As you ascend, listen to the gentle sounds of traditional hydraulic wheels and forest wildlife while observing residents engaged in their daily rice field activities.
The journey rewards photographers with stunning opportunities to capture the area's greenery and wildlife, culminating in breathtaking panoramic views from the summit that showcase the full majesty of this pristine landscape.
_Panoramic mountain views from Pu Luong's highest peaks_ _(Source: Canva)_

## 4. What to Do in Pu Luong Nature Reserve Vietnam
### 4.2. Take A Refreshing Swim at Hieu Waterfall
Situated in Hieu village, this magnificent cascading waterfall plunges approximately 800 meters, creating natural swimming pools perfect for relaxation and enjoying a peaceful snack break. The waterfall's multiple tiers provide various vantage points for photography and contemplation.
Getting to the waterfall is straightforward with a motorbike, as you can park close to the falls for less than VND 26,000 (USD 1). Car travelers will need to park near the entrance due to narrow access roads and walk approximately 10 minutes through scenic forest paths to reach this refreshing natural wonder.
_Crystal-clear waters at the 800-meter Hieu Waterfall in Pu Luong_ _(Source: Canva)_

## 4. What to Do in Pu Luong Nature Reserve Vietnam
### 4.3. Meet The Ethnic Minorities
The majority of communities within the reserve are Thai people, an ethnic group comprising two local branches: White Thai and Black Thai. These communities demonstrate remarkable skill in wet rice cultivation techniques passed down through generations, and their traditional homes showcase the distinctive raised stilt architecture adapted to the mountainous terrain.
Staying at one of the authentic homestays operated by these families provides an extraordinary opportunity to experience local customs firsthand, participate in daily activities, and gain a deeper understanding of their sustainable relationship with the natural environment.
_Traditional Thai stilt houses rise above the valley floor in Pu Luong, showcasing the distinctive architecture of local ethnic communities_ _(Source: Canva)_

## 4. What to Do in Pu Luong Nature Reserve Vietnam
### 4.4. Shop for Unique Souvenirs from Pho Doan Market
Operating every Thursday and Sunday morning, Pho Doan Market serves as a vibrant gathering place where local ethnic minorities including the Muong and Thai communities converge to buy and trade their goods. This colorful market offers an impressive variety of authentic items, from intricately handmade crafts and traditional clothing to region-specific products like aromatic spices and medicinal herbs.
The market atmosphere buzzes with local languages and provides excellent opportunities to interact with friendly vendors while discovering unique souvenirs that reflect the area's rich cultural heritage.
_Colorful displays of handmade crafts, traditional textiles, and local spices fill the bustling Pho Doan Market_ _(Source: Canva)_

## 4. What to Do in Pu Luong Nature Reserve Vietnam
### 4.5 Explore The Mysterious Bat Cave
Bat Cave (Hang Doi) represents the most remarkable geological formation in Pu Luong, having required more than 250 million years to achieve its current magnificent shape. Natural forces gradually wore down the surrounding karst landscape, leaving this striking feature carved deep within the central core of a river system. The same river that sculpted the cave continues to support local agriculture by providing essential water to the villages of Kho Muong and Ban Pon.
Within this mysterious cavern, several different bat species make their home, occasionally visible flying overhead. These bats play crucial roles in maintaining the area's ecological balance through insect population control and seed dispersal throughout the reserve.
